questions.question: Compare Delphinus and Dugongs based on adptations / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare Delphinus and Dugongs based on adptations [U] / [CO1]
  • Delphinus (dolphins) and dugongs are aquatic mammals, they have different adaptations based
  • on their distinct diets, habitats and ecological roles
  • Delphinus is a Carnivorous predator feeding on fishes and squid. They use sharp teeth to
  • grab prey and hunt cooperatively. Streamlined fusiform body, a stabilizing dorsal fin and a
  • powerful tail fluke helps to move fast. They rely on echolocation and interpret echoing sound
  • waves, allowing them to navigate in water. They also have sharp eyesight . They have
  • blowhole on top of the head, so they can breathe efficiently while swimming at high speeds.
  • Dugong is a bottom-dwelling coastal herbivore. They have a heavy, blimp-like body with
  • no dorsal fin and slow moving. They lack echolocation entirely. They have sensitive bristles
  • (vibrissae) on their snout to navigate and locate seagrass due to poor eyesight. They have
  • Valved nostrils on top of the snout which can be closed tightly when submerged, so they came
  • to the surface to breathe frequently. (Any2 differences-3 marks)

questions.question: Describe the optic lobe in pigeons. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the optic lobe in pigeons. (3 points-3 marks) [U] / [CO2]
  • • In Pigeons, two rounded optic lobes are present in midbrain, connected by a transverse
  • optic commissure.
  • • The two lobes are pushed towards the sides by the enlarged cerebrum and cerebellum.
  • • Optic lobes are large in size, in correlation with the keen sense of sight, essential for
  • flying and feeding.
  • • The right and left optic nerves arising from the optic lobes cross over each other and
  • fuse together, forming the optic chiasma.

questions.question: Give a note on the arterial system of Euphlyctis. / [CO2]

• Give a note on the arterial system of Euphlyctis. (brief account only) [U] / [CO2]
  • The arterial system in frog begins with the truncus arteriosus. The truncus divides into left and
  • right branches. Each branch now divides into three major vessels (1) The common carotid arch
  • supplies to the head region, is a short vessel and divides into two branches, external and internal
  • carotid (2) The systemic arch supplies to body and viscera is the longest of the three and has
  • the greatest distribution of blood. The two systemic arches curve dorsally and join with each
  • other behind the heart to form a common dorsal aorta which gives off many branches supplying
  • to different parts of the body . (3) Pulmocutaneous arch divides into two main branches,
  • pulmonary to the lung and cutaneous to the skin.

questions.question: Compare the forelimbs of Frog, Pigeon and Rabbit with respect to their functions. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare the forelimbs of Frog, Pigeon and Rabbit with respect to their functions.
  • [An]/[CO2]
  • Animal Primary Functions Structural Adaptations -2 points each
  • Frog Body support
  • • Supporting the body while resting on land.
  • • Radius and ulna are fused into a single radio-ulna bone to provide extra
  • structural strength for weight support.
  • Pigeon Flight
  • • Completely modified into wings to lift the body and propulsion through
  • the air. Wings are equipped with long flight feathers known as remiges
  • • Humerus, radius and ulna are well developed. Radius and ulna are
  • distinct, parallel to each other and joined only at their ends.
  • The bones are pneumatic (hollow) to reduce body weight.
  • • Distal bones (carpals and metacarpals) are reduced in number to four
  • and fused into a carpometacarpus to support flight feathers. The hand
  • has three digits only.
  • Rabbit

questions.question: Differentiate the respiratory mechanisms of frog, pigeon and rabbit. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate the respiratory mechanisms of frog, pigeon and rabbit. [U] / [CO2]
  • Respiratory mechanisms of pigeon: (3 marks)
  • Birds make use of two different respiratory mechanisms, one at rest and the other during flight.
  • In any case, inspiration is less active than expiration
  • In a resting bird, respiratory movements are brought about by ribs and stemum. During
  • inspiration, the intercostal muscles (muscles in between ribs) contract. As a result, the stemum
  • is moved down and the ribs are elevated. This releases the pressure over the lungs and at the
  • same time increases the volume of the body cavity. Consequently, fresh air from outside enters
  • the lungs and reaches the mesobronchus. From there a part of it flows to the inspiratory air
  • sacs. The rest flows to the endobronchi and parabronchi, reaches the bronchioles and gets
  • distributed all over the lungs. Gaseous exchange takes place in the parabronchi and bronchioles.
  • (if proper diagrammatic representation of double respiration is given only, give marks)
  • During expiration, sternum and ribs are raised by the contraction of abdominal muscles. As a
  • result, volume of the body cavity decreases and the lungs and inspiratory air sacs get pressed
  • against the ribs. Consequently, used air from the bronchioles is for ced out via ectobronchi,
  • primary bronchi and trachea. At the same time, inspiratory air sacs act as bellows to force air
  • from them back to the pulmonary air tubes. Most of the unused air from them flows to the
  • expiratory sacs through recurrent bronchi. A p ortion of it will flow to the endobronchi and
  • reach the bronchioles. During the next inspiration, unused air from the expiratory sacs will pass
  • to the bronchioles through endobronchi and parabronchi. Parabronchi and bronchioles receive
  • fresh air during inspiration and expiration, and no residual air is retained anywhere in the lungs.
  • So, within the lungs renewal of air and exchange of gases take place twice during every
  • respiratory cycle, one during ins piration and the other during expiration. This kind of
  • respiration is called double respiration. It supplies maximum amount of oxygen, for intense
  • metabolism, complete oxidation and increased energy release.
  • During flight, air can automatically rush in through the nostrils while the bird flies. The up and
  • down strokes of the wings and the movements of the flight muscles slightly move the vertebral
  • column up and down. This may cause changes in the body cavity and thereby help the
  • ventilation of lungs and air sacs.
  • Mechanism of respiration in rabbit (2 marks)
  • Lungs are enclosed in air tight pleural chambers in the thoracic cavity . The movement of ribs
  • and sternum increases the thoracic cavity from side to side and from above downward and the
  • straightening of the diaphragm causes its expansion from before backwards. When the thoracic
  • cavity thus increases in all the three dimensions, pleural cavities and lungs expand, creating a
  • low pressure inside the lungs. This causes the rushing of atmospheric air into the lungs, causing
  • inspiration. During expiration the external intercostal muscles and the muscles of the
  • diaphragm relax and the internal intercostal muscles contract. As a result, ribs, sternum and
  • diaphragm return to their original position. This decreases the volume of the thoracic and
  • pleural cavities and the lungs, causing expiration.
  • (If respiratory mechanisms of pigeon and rabbit is written, give marks)

questions.question: Explain the digestive system of pigeon and compare it with that of frog. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the digestive system of pigeon and compare it with that of frog. [U] / [CO2]
  • Digestive system comprises the alimentary canal and the glands associated with it. Alimentary
  • canal is a longcoiled tube and differentiated into several functionally different regions, such as
  • buccal cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, crop, stomach, duodenum, ileum and rectum which opens
  • to the cloaca. Buccal cavity is bounded above and below by the toothless horny beak. On the
  • buccal floor is the pointed tongue. It contains mucous glands and scanty taste buds. Buccal roof
  • is formed by the palate, which is a partition between the buccal and nasal cavitie s. Salivary
  • glands are absent. But there are a few mucus secreting buccal glands. Their secretion moistens
  • the food. Buccal cavity is followed by the pharynx. Pharynx leads to the long, tubular and
  • distensible oesophagus or gullet. It passes down the neck and terminally enlarges to a thin -
  • walled sac or reservoir, known as crop. The crop serves three purposes, namely (i) storage of
  • large amount of ingested food to enable the bird to feed quickly (ii) maceration (softening) of
  • the food by storage (iii) moistening of the food. Pigeons are unique in producing a white
  • proteinaceous and fatty secretion, called 'pigeon's milk' or 'crop milk'. It is produced in both
  • the sexes by a pair of crop glands during breeding season and used to nourish the squabs until
  • they are able to feed upon grains. Crop leads to the stomach. Stomach has two portions, fore-
  • stomach or Proventriculus is the tubular and glandular initial part concerned with enzyme
  • production and gizzard or hind-stomach is the thick-walled and muscular terminal part, serves
  • as a muscular mill for crushing and grinding the food. It is equipped with a horny internal lining
  • with tooth-like ridges for crushing the food. Gizzard leads to the small intestine through a small
  • passage called pylorus, guarded by a pyloric sphincter. Small intestine has two parts, duodenum
  • is a short and bent part and ileum is a long and coiled tube. In between the two duodenal limbs
  • lies the pancreas. Joining the duodenum is a bile ducts and pancreatic ducts. The internal lining
  • of the ileum is produced into numerous villi to increase the absorptive area. Following the
  • ileum is the short rectum that represents the large intestine. At the junction of ileum and rectum
  • is a pair of blind pouches, called rectal caeca or colic caeca. Terminally, rectum opens to the
  • cloaca. This opening is guarded by a muscular sphincter, called anal sphincter. Cloaca has three
  • linear compartments, namely coprodaeum, urodaeum and proctodaeum (or vestibule).
  • Coprodaeum receives the rectum, urodaeum receives the urinary and genital ducts, and
  • proctodaeum opens to the outside by the cloacal opening or vent.
  • Digestive glands: Buccal glands, gastric glands, intestinal glands, liver and pancreas are the
  • major glands associated with the alimentary canal. Buccal glands are not true salivary glands,
  • secrete enzyme-free mucus to moisten the food. Gastric glands are the glandular pits in the
  • mucous membrane of proventriculus. They secrete gastric juice, which contains HCl and the
  • proteolytic enzyme pepsin. Intestinal glands are seen in the mucous membrane of ileum. They
  • secrete intestinal juice, which contains proteolytic, amylolytic and lipolytic enzymes. Liver is
  • a bilobed gland, secretes the alkaline bile. Gall bladder is absent in adult pigeons. Pancreas is
  • a heterocrine gland, with exocrine secretion is called pancreatic juice. It is discharged to the
  • the duodenum through three pancreatic ducts. Pancreatic juice contains protein -splitting,
  • carbohydrate-splitting and fat-splitting enzymes.
  • Digestive system o f Frog: Frog has a very wide mouth bordered by immovable lips.
  • Protrusible, glandular sticky tongue is used in capturing the prey. In frogs, the base of the
  • tongue is attached anteriorly at the margin of the jaw and the free end is folded back on the
  • floor of the mouth when at rest. Teeth are confined to the upper jaw and vomers. Lower jaw is
  • toothless. Dentition is polyphyodont, homodont and acrodont. The oesophagus is extremely
  • short. In frog the cardiac end of the stomach is wide and the pyloric end is short and narrow.
  • Small intestine is coiled and large intestine is short and straight. Villi appear for the first time
  • in amphibians. An ileocolic valve is present between small and large intestines.The large
  • intestine opens into the cloaca.
  • Digestive glands: Only mucous glands are present in the buccal cavity. Salivary glands are
  • absent. Liver is large and well developed. Gall bladder is present. Pancreas is compact and lies
  • in the mesentery stretching between the duodenum and the stomach.
  • (Digestive system of pigeon-3marks; frog -2 mark)

• Explain how the skin of a Frog helps in cutaneous respiration and water balance.
  • / [CO2] (Any 5 points-5 marks)
  • • Skin is smooth, slimy and glandular with mucus glands
  • • Skin is naked without exoskeleton/scales.
  • • Skin is richly supplied with blood capillaries that lies directly beneath the surface and
  • is permeable to gases.
  • • Before oxygen can diffuse into blood it must first be dissolved in water and that is why
  • frogs always stay near water to keep their skin moist. It is further kept moist by secretion
  • of mucus from its glands.
  • • cutaneous respiration operates continuously serving as the primary method all the time
  • when a frog is underwater or hibernating.
  • • Frogs absorb water directly through their skin. The skin on a frog's lower belly and
  • thighs—often called the pelvic patch —is specially adapted with high permeability to
  • rapidly pull in moisture from damp soil, bodies of water.
  • • Mucus secretions helps to slow down excessive evaporation, if frogs kept in dry air for
  • too long. [5x4 = 20]
